$comment: Seed for the knowledge_rule table — the curated, conflict-resolved judgment rules the financing engine CITES. Every slug emitted by lib/financing/recommend.ts must exist here (guaranteed by knowledge.coverage.test.ts), so a recommendation's citation always resolves to real, auditable text. Sourced from docs/knowledge-base/Concepts/creative-finance.md + RESEARCH-FINDINGS.md Stream 3. Informational, not legal advice.

rules.condition: Seller has little/no equity or is distressed (NEED), and holds a below-market-rate loan.
rules.recommendation: Subject-To: take over the existing low-rate mortgage with no money down. From the seller's side you effectively wrote the ~check they'd otherwise owe at closing.

rules.condition: Seller has high equity and wants top dollar + to defer capital gains (GREED); long-held appreciated asset.
rules.recommendation: Seller Finance: they carry the note over time → higher price + monthly income + capital-gains deferral; you skip the bank and preserve trust capital for more doors.

rules.condition: Mixed equity: some assumable low-rate debt plus a meaningful equity gap.
rules.recommendation: Hybrid: subject-to the existing loan + a seller carry on the equity gap. Carries BOTH the due-on-sale and seller-finance constraints.

rules.condition: Seller-financed deal layered over an existing underlying loan.
rules.recommendation: Wraparound: a seller-finance note that 'wraps' the underlying mortgage. Combines seller-finance economics with due-on-sale exposure; some states require specific disclosures.

rules.condition: Any transfer of a property whose mortgage stays in the seller's name (subject-to / wrap).
rules.recommendation: Due-on-sale (12 U.S.C. §1701j-3) lets the lender CALL the loan on transfer — historically rare on a performing loan, but the rate gap (3% vs 7%) now gives lenders a real incentive. Insurance changes are the most common way the transfer is discovered.

rules.condition: Claim that a land trust + Garn-St.-Germain exempts a subject-to transfer from due-on-sale.
rules.recommendation: FALSE for an investor acquisition. The §1701j-3(d)(8) trust exception protects a borrower moving THEIR OWN property into a trust in which they remain beneficiary; once beneficial interest is assigned to the investor/their LLC, the protection evaporates. A land trust may hide the transfer; it does not legally exempt it. → attorney.

rules.condition: Seller financing where the buyer is a non-occupant investor (vs a consumer-occupant).
rules.recommendation: Investor/non-occupant buyers are generally OUTSIDE the consumer loan-originator + ability-to-repay rules. A consumer-occupant must fit the 1-property exclusion (natural person/TRUST only — an LLC cannot) or 3-property exclusion (entities OK, ATR required). State SAFE Act can be stricter.
